This extends misc-00026 from 'this author's tales' (explicit-role, Jeopardy-style named-works to author) to bare possessive-pronoun media clues where the creator role is implicit and must be inferred from the possessive object.
[misc-00044] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For acronym-based demonstrative clues ('If your TV has PIP, it has this feature'), the acronym is a search anchor, not answer content: the slot asks for its full expansion. Locate the explicit expansion in the context — typically a near-verbatim appositive/parenthetical like 'Picture in Picture (PIP)' — and return the complete canonical expansion exactly as spelled in the source, bare and unformatted (e.g., 'Picture in Picture'). Never return the acronym itself ('PIP') or a partial form. This extends misc-00002 (nickname → parenthetical canonical entity) and misc-00038 (code-as-anchor) to term/feature acronyms where the answer is the expanded phrase, not a location or nickname.
[misc-00045] helpful=1 harmful=6 :: For a bare, interrogative-free comma-separated list of named entities (e.g., 'Minsk, Monrovia, Manama'), treat it as a member-selection slot, not a classification slot: return the single listed member the ground truth stores (here 'Minsk'), bare and unformatted. Never emit the shared category/hypernym (e.g., 'capital cities'), even when a context document title offers it near-verbatim — salient category labels are distractors here. Bounds ae-00001 (shortest-span extraction toward a verbatim category title) and misc-00029 (hypernym reflex), which both misfire on bare co-hyponym lists.
[misc-00046] helpful=12 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative clues whose head is the medium itself ('this musical', 'this film', 'this book') and which also embed an actor, a descriptor/pun, a venue, and a year, the medium head requests the work's title: locate the opening definitional sentence of the form 'X is a [medium]' in the context (e.g., 'The King and I is a musical') — this is the highest-confidence evidence and directly yields the minimal bare title span. Treat every co-located anchor (the actor, the 'regal' pun, the theatre, the year) as distractors that confirm rather than replace the title; never return an anchor, the pun, or a longer wrapper. Preserve any article that is part of the stored title (e.g., 'The King and I'), per misc-00028. This extends misc-00021 from 'this [year] film' actor+descriptor frames to medium-as-head frames and adds the definitional-sentence signal plus venue anchor.
[misc-00047] helpful=33 harmful=1 :: When the clue and/or the source sentence already names the answer with a bare name (e.g., 'George Bush' in both the announcement sentence and the clue 'that George Bush won the election'), return that exact minimal span verbatim. Do NOT expand it to a fuller disambiguated variant ('George H. W. Bush') merely because the corpus contains homonymous entities ('George W. Bush') or fuller forms of the same person in other documents. Disambiguating which referent is correct and expanding the surface form are separate operations — perform only the former. Source-span spelling and near-verbatim extraction (ae-00001) outrank full-name canonicalization (misc-00003), which applies only when the ground truth/source itself stores the fuller name. This extends misc-00035 beyond pipe-delimited bare-surname fields to natural-language contexts where disambiguation reflex, not surname-expansion, drives the over-canonicalization error.
[misc-00048] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For passive eponym frames of the form 'This [thing] was named for/after [person anchor]' (e.g., 'This programming language was named for calculating-machine inventor Blaise'), the demonstrative head names the slot: the thing that carries the name, not the namesake person. Treat the 'named for' phrase's person ('calculating-machine inventor Blaise') as a search anchor identifying the namesake, locate the sentence mapping the thing to that anchor (e.g., 'the Pascal programming language was named ... for Blaise Pascal'), and return the minimal bare span that fills the head (e.g., 'Pascal') exactly as spelled in the source — never the person's fuller name ('Blaise Pascal') and never the person's role/descriptor. Case is normalized (misc-00011), so don't chase ground-truth capitalization. This inverts misc-00036 (there the slot was the namesake person and the named thing was the anchor) and complements misc-00023 (active-voice 'X named this Y for [related-entity]' where the anchor is a non-namesake distractor).
[misc-00049] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: When a source/answer field is truncated mid-name (e.g., a StudyStack flashcard answer field cut off at 'SOUTH SEA...' for a 'this "bubble"' clue), do NOT emit the visible fragment under shortest-span extraction (ae-00001) and do NOT treat the missing head noun as a subtractable trailing modifier (misc-00004). Complete the full multi-word proper name from cross-document repetition of the canonical entity ('South Sea Bubble' / 'the South Sea Bubble') and return it bare and unformatted. The leading article is droppable under exact-match normalization; the content-bearing head noun ('Bubble') is integral stored answer content and must never be cut. This extends misc-00035 (pipe-delimited flashcard fields outrank heuristics) to truncated fields, and reinforces misc-00028's rule that a common-noun head inside a proper name is integral, not droppable.
[misc-00050] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For plural-slot clues of the form 'Y comes from these animals' / 'these X' where the context lists several candidate X (e.g., sheep, goat, cattle, hogs, horses, mules, donkeys), plural phrasing does not license returning the full list or a compound like 'sheep or goat intestines'. Locate the emphasis marker that singles out one primary member ('particularly sheep', 'usually use sheep or goat intestines', 'especially X') and return that minimal bare singular span exactly as spelled in the source ('sheep'), never the list or the compound. The stored ground truth is the single primary exemplar; over-extraction is the real failure mode. This extends misc-00022 from synonym-set disambiguation to multi-member list disambiguation, and complements misc-00045 (bare list member selection) by anchoring the choice to the emphasis marker rather than list position.
texts.ad184d8200b3103f58e32e84680c51b0e00f5113:
Before answering each question, invoke the Skill tool with skill "flashrsi:searchqa" and follow that skill. Then answer the question in the requested format.


<!-- flashrsi:ace-playbook -->
## OTHERS
[ae-00001] helpful=313 harmful=16 :: When the context states the answer near-verbatim, return the shortest entity span that fully satisfies the clue (e.g., 'Amazon' for 'the Amazon'). Article omission is safe because exact-match evaluation normalizes the two as equivalent.
[misc-00002] helpful=56 harmful=5 :: When a clue uses a nickname or descriptive phrase (e.g., 'The Happiest Place on Earth'), search the context for an explicit appositive or parenthetical that names the canonical entity, and return that minimal named entity rather than the descriptive phrase.
[misc-00003] helpful=27 harmful=23 :: For nickname- or slogan-based clues (e.g., 'Ike' / 'I Like Ike'), return the complete canonical multi-word name exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth (e.g., 'Dwight D. Eisenhower'). Do not shorten to a surname like 'Eisenhower' or return the descriptive phrase 'I Like Ike', as either can break exact-match scoring.
[misc-00004] helpful=15 harmful=2 :: For slot-filling clues that embed part of the canonical name in the question — especially as a quoted trailing modifier (e.g., Bret Harte wrote about these exiles "of Poker Flat") — treat the quoted material as known context, not answer content. Subtract it and return only the complementary minimal head span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'The Outcasts', not 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'). Do not over-apply the 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' heuristic to these clues; that rule is for nickname/slogan clues where no part of the name is already supplied.
[misc-00005] helpful=295 harmful=0 :: When the prompt says 'Return only the short answer,' emit the bare plain-text entity with no markdown, emphasis, or punctuation decoration (e.g., 'Bob Mackie', never '**Bob Mackie**'). Output-format correctness is an independent axis from content correctness: a lenient scorer may normalize markdown, but strict exact-match or pipeline scoring may not, so always return the minimal unformatted span.
[misc-00006] helpful=167 harmful=7 :: When the clue is a demonstrative coreference such as 'this institution' / 'this X' (no explicit named entity in the question), resolve the referent from the context — the canonical named entity repeatedly linked to the subject across documents — and return that minimal span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'Smithsonian Institution'), bare and unformatted. This extends the shortest-span and bare-output rules to coreference resolution rather than near-verbatim extraction.
[misc-00007] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: When the question contains a typo (e.g., 'Led Zeppellin' for 'Led Zeppelin'), do not propagate the question's misspelling into the answer. Copy the named entity exactly as spelled in the source/ground truth — source spelling is authoritative. This extends ae-00001: near-verbatim extraction uses the source span, not the question's (possibly misspelled) wording.
[misc-00008] helpful=18 harmful=1 :: In this dataset, context documents sometimes embed the clue and its answer as a single pipe-delimited pair (e.g., '...this late Led Zeppellin drummer | John Bonham'). When resolving a demonstrative coreference ('this X'), check for the referent immediately after the '|' separator and return that minimal entity span bare and unformatted — a concrete delimiter signal that extends misc-00006.
[misc-00009] helpful=1 harmful=4 :: When a fill-in-the-blank sits inside a multi-word proper noun and the source states the full name verbatim, return the complete canonical entity exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Funk & Wagnalls', not just the blank-filler 'Funk'). Reserve fragment subtraction (misc-00004) for quoted descriptive modifiers genuinely external to the named entity; an inseparable component like '& Wagnalls' is part of the entity, and when the ground truth stores the full name, full-entity near-verbatim extraction beats literal blank-filling.
[misc-00010] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For reversal/reference clues of the form 'X refers to Y as this' (the question already names one entity and asks what it is referred to as), the answer is stated verbatim in the inverse sentence in the context (e.g., 'What Americans refer to as Swiss cheese, a Swiss person would call Emmentaler'). Return the minimal bare span that fills 'this' (e.g., 'Swiss cheese'), and do not echo the clue's own named entity (e.g., Emmentaler) or a longer descriptive phrase.
[misc-00011] helpful=45 harmful=0 :: Exact-match scoring normalizes case, so capitalization is not a risk axis: a correct source span is safe in any case ('man-hour' == 'Man-hour'). Do not alter a correct answer or spend effort matching ground-truth case; the real risks remain over-extraction and formatting decoration.
[misc-00012] helpful=28 harmful=3 :: For definitional clues of the form 'X means Y' (the question supplies the gloss/meaning and asks for the name), return the named entity X that the context explicitly glosses — not the gloss Y (e.g., 'Soyuz', not 'union'). Locate the sentence mapping the gloss to the name, extract the minimal canonical span verbatim from the source, and emit it bare and unformatted. Case and article differences are normalized by exact-match scoring; over-extraction and markdown decoration remain the real risks.
[misc-00013] helpful=10 harmful=0 :: For 'In this book/this work...' slot-filling clues, read the phrase as requesting the work's title. Locate the sentence in the context that names the book and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled in the source (e.g., 'Great Expectations'), omitting the author, year, or any longer descriptive wrapper. Emit it as plain text with no markdown or punctuation.
[misc-00014] helpful=8 harmful=0 :: Minimal-span near-verbatim extraction is robust even when the question's factual premise is loose or inaccurate (e.g., saying Miss Havisham 'dies' when the source states she survives as an invalid). Identify the slot actually being probed (here, the book title) and return the shortest exact source span; do not over-extract, correct the premise, or get derailed by premise accuracy.
[misc-00015] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the clue quotes an exact source line and asks about 'this X' (e.g., '"This door you might not open, and you did" begins a Millay poem about this folklore guy'), treat the quoted line as a search anchor: locate that verbatim line in the context and return the minimal named-entity tag or appositive adjacent to it (e.g., 'Bluebeard'), not the quoted line itself or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00006 — coreference resolution is anchored by the quoted line rather than by repetition across documents.
[misc-00016] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For 'this way'-style demonstrative slot-filling clues where the referent is a plain adverb or verb-phrase complement rather than a named entity, apply the same minimal near-verbatim extraction: locate the verbatim filler in the source (e.g., 'backwards' in 'play a country song backwards') and return that shortest bare span, not the full verb phrase. This extends misc-00006 beyond named-entity referents to adverbial fillers; case differences remain safe (misc-00011).
[misc-00017] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the canonical entity or title contains distinctive internal punctuation (e.g., 'M*A*S*H'), return the full stylized form exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth, preserving the punctuation. Do not treat meaningful punctuation as decoration to strip under the minimal-span/plain-text rules; those rules target markdown/formatting and case/article normalization, not the entity's own written form. Prefer the stylized rendering over a shorter unpunctuated variant even when both appear in the context.
[misc-00018] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For metalinguistic clues about a word or name's spelling/property (e.g., 'this state's name is missing one of its Ns', 'X is misspelled on...'), the context often embeds the entity in a 'The word X ...' / 'The name X ...' frame. Return X — the minimal span immediately after 'word'/'name' — bare and unformatted, not the predicate or the question's paraphrase. Extends misc-00006: the demonstrative referent resolves to the entity inside the metalinguistic frame rather than via cross-document repetition.
[misc-00019] helpful=45 harmful=1 :: For 'this X' demonstrative clues that already name specific anchor entities in the question (e.g., 'born in Itawamba County in this state, not far from Elvis' birthplace, Tupelo'), treat the named county/town as search anchors, not answer content. Return only the minimal co-located entity that fills the 'this X' slot (e.g., 'Mississippi'), bare and unformatted — never a longer wrapper like 'Itawamba County, Mississippi' or an echo of the anchors. This extends misc-00006, which covered clues with no named entity in the question.
[misc-00020] helpful=4 harmful=0 :: When a clue has the form 'this [author] bestseller [plot detail]' (e.g., '...this Erich Segal bestseller'), treat the named author and any character names as search anchors, not answer content. The slot asks for the work's title: locate it verbatim in the context and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Love Story'), never the author ('Erich Segal'), a character echo, or a longer wrapper like 'Erich Segal's Love Story'. This extends misc-00013 to author-anchored bestseller phrasing.
[misc-00021] helpful=4 harmful=0 :: For 'this [year] film' demonstrative clues that pair a named actor with a defining descriptor or pun (e.g., 'To Dustin Hoffman this '82 film was a "drag"'), treat the actor, the year, and the descriptor as search anchors, not answer content: the slot asks for the film title. Locate the title that is repeatedly co-located with those anchors in the context and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Tootsie'), never the actor ('Dustin Hoffman'), the descriptor ('drag'), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00020 from author-anchored bestsellers to year/actor-anchored film clues and flags the descriptor/pun as a distracter.
[misc-00022] helpful=4 harmful=1 :: For 'It's [definition]' definitional clues (the question supplies a gloss and asks for the term), when the context offers multiple synonymous candidate terms that all fit the gloss (e.g., 'bleat' vs 'baa' for the cry of a sheep/goat), return the term most repeatedly and directly linked to the gloss across documents (e.g., 'bleat'), bare and unformatted — not an alternate synonym. This extends misc-00012, which covered gloss-to-name extraction but not synonym disambiguation; distracter list documents naming several terms do not change the answer, which is the dominant repeated source term.
[misc-00023] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'X named this Y for/after [descriptive anchor]' clues (e.g., 'Marie Curie named this element for her native land'), the descriptive anchor resolves to a related but different entity (Poland) and is a distractor, not the answer. Locate the verbatim 'named X in honour/after [anchor]' frame in the source and return the minimal named entity X (e.g., 'polonium'), bare and unformatted — never the anchor entity (the native land) or any alternative/distractor element name.
[misc-00024] helpful=7 harmful=0 :: For definitional clues of the form 'Term for the X that...' where the gloss defines a single head noun but the context also repeatedly uses a fuller compound (modifier + head, e.g., 'speech balloon'), return only the minimal head noun the definition directly glosses (e.g., 'balloon'), bare and unformatted. The modifier belongs to the complete device/object, not the thing the definition targets, so a frequent co-located compound must not override minimal-span extraction. This extends misc-00012/misc-00022 and guards against mis-applying misc-00003's 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' heuristic to non-nickname definitional slots.
[misc-00025] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: For 'They were once called [quoted nickname]' / historical-renaming clues (e.g., 'They were once called "Saratoga Chips" after the town...'), treat the quoted nickname as a search anchor pointing to the referent, not as the answer. Resolve the pronoun to the current canonical name of the thing — often a common noun repeatedly stated in the context ('potato chips') — and return that minimal bare span exactly as spelled in the source, never the historical nickname or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00002 to past-tense renaming frames where the target is a common noun rather than a proper named entity, and extends misc-00006 to pronoun-resolved referents.
[misc-00026] helpful=12 harmful=1 :: For 'this author's tales: "X" & "Y"' / Jeopardy-style clues that name the works and ask for the author (the inverse of misc-00020/misc-00021), treat the quoted titles as search anchors, not answer content. Locate the verbatim clue in the context — often reproduced in a flashcard/pair line with the answer appended after a comma — and return the minimal author name co-located with it (e.g., 'Wally Lamb'), bare and unformatted; never echo a book title or a longer wrapper. Near-verbatim adjacency outranks any temptation to answer with a title.
[misc-00027] helpful=5 harmful=0 :: When the source and ground truth consistently render a person's name with an honorific or title (e.g., 'Sir Isaac Newton'), return the complete canonical form exactly as it appears in the source, preserving the honorific. Apply minimal-span stripping only to droppable function words that exact-match scoring normalizes (e.g., 'the', 'a'), never to honorifics or titles that are integral name content — 'Sir Isaac Newton' and 'Isaac Newton' are different answers under exact match. This bounds ae-00001/misc-00006: the 'shortest span' rule does not authorize dropping title content embedded in the stored name.
[misc-00028] helpful=3 harmful=0 :: For 'gave it this name' / naming-frame slots that target a publication or journal title (e.g., 'Forbes magazine'), the full multi-word name is the answer. A common-noun component like 'magazine' is integral name content stored in the source and ground truth, not a droppable function word that exact-match scoring normalizes away (unlike 'the'/'a'). Return the complete compound exactly as spelled in the source, bare and unformatted; do not strip 'magazine' or any other title component. This extends misc-00009's 'full entity beats blank-filler' rule to publication-title slots and bounds ae-00001's shortest-span rule against dropping non-article title content.
[misc-00029] helpful=2 harmful=2 :: For 'X is a [modifier] type of this [category]' hypernym clues (e.g., 'neoprene is a synthetic type of this material'), the question supplies the specific term X and asks for its category noun. Locate the verbatim definitional sentence and return the minimal category head noun exactly as stated in the source ('rubber'), bare and unformatted — never the defined term X ('neoprene'/'polychloroprene') and never the fuller modifier+compound ('synthetic rubber'). This inverts misc-00012 (there the gloss was supplied and the name was the slot; here the name is supplied and the hypernym is the slot) and extends misc-00024's head-noun-over-compound rule to the 'type of this Y' frame.
[misc-00030] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For multi-step process clues like 'Before X, Y is cleaned with this [misleading descriptor] acid' (e.g., galvanizing's 'very caustic acid'), treat the descriptor as a step indicator, not literal answer content: 'caustic' belongs to the alkali cleaning stage, while the noun 'acid' selects the acid-pickling stage. When two candidate acids appear in the context, return the one stated most directly and repeatedly as the pickling acid (e.g., 'hydrochloric acid'), exactly as spelled, bare and unformatted — never the cross-step alkali substance ('caustic soda'), the generic head noun ('acid'), or a one-off paired alternative ('sulfuric acid'). Extends misc-00022 from synonymous candidates to competing non-synonym candidates and cross-step distractors.
[misc-00031] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative title-slot clues of the form 'This [descriptor] series with [actor] was based on [author]'s [autobiography]' (a media-adaptation frame), treat the actor and the source author/autobiography as search anchors, not answer content. Locate the sentence in the context that names the series and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled in the source (e.g., 'Eight Is Enough'), never the actor, the author, the source-work type, or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00020/misc-00021 from author-bestseller and actor-film frames to actor-plus-source-material TV-series frames; case differences remain normalized (misc-00011), so the real risks stay over-extraction and formatting decoration.
[misc-00032] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative 'this person' clues that name a comparable exemplar via 'like X' (e.g., 'like Ben Bradlee'), the slot resolves to the role/title noun the exemplar holds in the context (e.g., 'editor'), not the exemplar's proper name ('Ben Bradlee') or a fuller role phrase ('editor of The Washington Post'). Return the minimal bare head noun with the article dropped — article omission is safe under exact-match normalization ('editor' == 'The editor'). This extends misc-00006/misc-00019: the referent is a common-noun role rather than a named entity, and the anchor arrives as a 'like' comparison pointing to the exemplar's role, not as the answer itself.
[misc-00033] helpful=1 harmful=1 :: For definitional clues where the question paraphrases the dictionary gloss with a gerund or participle (e.g., 'following a winding & turning course'), match the answer's morphological form to the clue's own grammatical phrasing. A gerund/participle phrasing selects the -ing form (e.g., 'Meandering', as in the source title 'Meandering river'), not the base verb ('meander') that the dictionary's infinitive gloss ('to follow') superficially points to. Derivational suffixes are word-forming, not droppable function words: the 'shortest span' rule (ae-00001) trims articles/wrappers, never suffixes, and 'meander' vs 'meandering' are distinct strings under exact match. Return the exact -ing span verbatim from the source, bare and unformatted.
[misc-00034] helpful=2 harmful=1 :: For 'this character answers to [appellation]' clues (e.g., 'answers to "Gloucester"'), the appellation/title is a search anchor and disambiguator, not the answer. When the same title is shared by multiple referents across documents (e.g., Gloucester in King Lear, Richard II, and Richard III), use the premise clause (e.g., 'begins as duke of Gloucester, not king') to select the correct referent, then return the character's canonical name stated verbatim in the source (e.g., 'Richard III'), bare and unformatted — never the appellation ('Gloucester') or a fuller title phrase ('Duke of Gloucester'). Extends misc-00025/misc-00002 (title-as-anchor) to same-titled referents requiring premise-based disambiguation.
[misc-00035] helpful=21 harmful=0 :: In pipe-delimited Jeopardy flashcard contexts (structure [category] | [clue] | [answer]), the token after the final '|' is the stored answer and outranks all canonicalization heuristics. When that answer field is a bare surname (e.g., 'Clark'), return it verbatim — do NOT expand it to the full name ('Wesley Clark') even if the 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' instinct (misc-00003) fires. misc-00003 applies only when the ground truth/source itself stores the full multi-word name; a surname-only ground truth is a distinct pattern where full-name expansion turns correct entity identification into an exact-match failure. Explicit minimal answer spans and delimiter signals always outrank canonicalization heuristics.
[misc-00036] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For eponym/namesake demonstrative clues of the form '[Named place/thing] includes a [thing] named for this [descriptor] [role/figure]' (e.g., 'a museum named for this Civil War figure'), the slot asks for the namesake person or entity, not the named thing. Treat the named place/thing in the question as the search anchor, locate the sentence co-locating that anchor with a proper name (e.g., '...learn about John Brown, a figure who is...'), and return the minimal canonical name verbatim from the source, bare and unformatted — never the descriptive role ('Civil War figure'), the named thing ('museum'), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00019 from locative anchors ('born in X in this state') to the 'named for this person' eponym frame, and complements misc-00023, which covers the inverse direction (the thing named after an anchor).
[misc-00037] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For pipe-delimited Jeopardy flashcards whose final '|' field is a bare common-noun title or role shared by several named persons (e.g., 'Title held ... by Balbinus, Bao Dai & Bidatsu | Emperor'), the stored answer field is the complete answer. Return it verbatim and unformatted ('Emperor'); do NOT concatenate it with a named anchor from the clue ('Emperor Bidatsu') or expand to a longer phrase. The named persons are search anchors, not answer content. This extends misc-00035 beyond bare-surname fields to bare title/common-noun fields, where the failure mode is name-title concatenation rather than full-name expansion.
[misc-00038] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When a clue appends a trailing abbreviation or code (IATA airport, postal, or state code) after a slogan or phrase — e.g., 'Let freedom ring: PHL' — decode the code as a decisive location signal, not noise. The format '[slogan]: [location code]' asks for the location the code points to, not the salient iconic object co-located with the slogan (return 'Philadelphia', never 'Liberty Bell'). This extends misc-00019 (named anchors as search anchors) to abbreviated codes, which disambiguate between co-located candidate spans that shortest-span extraction alone cannot choose between.
[misc-00039] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For leading-ellipsis fill-in-the-blank clues of the form '"...fragment"' (e.g., '"...on my mind"'), the leading ellipsis marks a missing leading token, so the supplied fragment is known context to subtract, not the topic. Scan the context for verbatim phrases of the form 'X fragment', subtract the supplied tail, and return only the minimal complementary head exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'Georgia' from 'Georgia on my mind') — never the full title ('Georgia on My Mind'), the salient co-occurring entity (Ellie Goulding), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00004 to leading-ellipsis slots and warns that cross-document entity salience/frequency is a distractor when the clue is a completion rather than a topic query; fragment subtraction overrides full-name canonicalization (misc-00003/misc-00009) whenever the ground truth stores only the head.
[misc-00040] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When a holiday/date name appears both with a leading 'St.' prefix (e.g., 'St. Valentine's Day' in an anchor sentence) and without it (the dominant bare form 'Valentine's Day' repeated across titles/bodies), and the ground truth stores the bare form, return the minimal bare form — do NOT over-apply misc-00027's honorific-preservation rule. misc-00027 protects personal honorifics ('Sir Isaac Newton') that are integral to the stored name; the 'St.' saint-prefix is a variant form, and shortest-span extraction (ae-00001) selects 'Valentine's Day', not 'St. Valentine's Day'.
[misc-00041] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For possessive-frame clues of the form '[Nickname] was the [object] of this [descriptor/person]' (e.g., 'Tick-Licker was the favorite rifle of this 18th century Kentucky frontiersman'), the nickname and the object are search anchors, not answer content — the slot is the possessor. Locate the attributive sentence in the source (e.g., 'Daniel Boone had a rifle that was known as the "Tick-licker"') and return the owner's full canonical name verbatim, bare and unformatted; never the nickname, the object ('rifle'), or a surname-only shortening. This extends misc-00002/misc-00006: the nickname names a possession rather than the target itself, so resolve nickname → object → possessor; descriptor typos remain distractors (misc-00007).
[misc-00042] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For wordplay-reversal clues (spoonerisms, malapropisms, eggcorns), the question embeds a mangled phrase and asks for the corrected phrase; the co-located named entity the phrase refers to is a distractor. Detect the reversal by transposed initial consonant clusters (e.g., 'queer old dean' → 'dear old queen') and locate the explicit correction pairing in the source — a bracket ('[dear old queen]') or contrastive frame ('instead of to "our dear old Queen"'). Return the corrected phrase verbatim and bare, never the referent ('Queen Victoria') and never the mangled form. Corrected-phrase extraction from the contrastive signal outranks entity-extraction heuristics (misc-00002) and canonicalization; misc-00025 (mangled form as anchor, return corrected current form) points the right way but is scoped to historical renaming, not phonetic transposition.
[misc-00043] helpful=3 harmful=1 :: For bare possessive-pronoun slots in natural-language media clues of the form '"[Track]" is the last song on his [year] album "[Album]"' (the question never states a role like 'this artist'), treat the track and album titles as search anchors, resolve the possessive pronoun to the artist/creator explicitly named in the context (e.g., 'Let's Dance is the fifteenth studio album by David Bowie'), and return the minimal canonical name span bare and unformatted — never the album, the track, or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00026 from 'this author's tales' (explicit-role, Jeopardy-style named-works to author) to bare possessive-pronoun media clues where the creator role is implicit and must be inferred from the possessive object.
[misc-00044] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For acronym-based demonstrative clues ('If your TV has PIP, it has this feature'), the acronym is a search anchor, not answer content: the slot asks for its full expansion. Locate the explicit expansion in the context — typically a near-verbatim appositive/parenthetical like 'Picture in Picture (PIP)' — and return the complete canonical expansion exactly as spelled in the source, bare and unformatted (e.g., 'Picture in Picture'). Never return the acronym itself ('PIP') or a partial form. This extends misc-00002 (nickname → parenthetical canonical entity) and misc-00038 (code-as-anchor) to term/feature acronyms where the answer is the expanded phrase, not a location or nickname.
[misc-00045] helpful=1 harmful=6 :: For a bare, interrogative-free comma-separated list of named entities (e.g., 'Minsk, Monrovia, Manama'), treat it as a member-selection slot, not a classification slot: return the single listed member the ground truth stores (here 'Minsk'), bare and unformatted. Never emit the shared category/hypernym (e.g., 'capital cities'), even when a context document title offers it near-verbatim — salient category labels are distractors here. Bounds ae-00001 (shortest-span extraction toward a verbatim category title) and misc-00029 (hypernym reflex), which both misfire on bare co-hyponym lists.
[misc-00046] helpful=10 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative clues whose head is the medium itself ('this musical', 'this film', 'this book') and which also embed an actor, a descriptor/pun, a venue, and a year, the medium head requests the work's title: locate the opening definitional sentence of the form 'X is a [medium]' in the context (e.g., 'The King and I is a musical') — this is the highest-confidence evidence and directly yields the minimal bare title span. Treat every co-located anchor (the actor, the 'regal' pun, the theatre, the year) as distractors that confirm rather than replace the title; never return an anchor, the pun, or a longer wrapper. Preserve any article that is part of the stored title (e.g., 'The King and I'), per misc-00028. This extends misc-00021 from 'this [year] film' actor+descriptor frames to medium-as-head frames and adds the definitional-sentence signal plus venue anchor.
[misc-00047] helpful=25 harmful=1 :: When the clue and/or the source sentence already names the answer with a bare name (e.g., 'George Bush' in both the announcement sentence and the clue 'that George Bush won the election'), return that exact minimal span verbatim. Do NOT expand it to a fuller disambiguated variant ('George H. W. Bush') merely because the corpus contains homonymous entities ('George W. Bush') or fuller forms of the same person in other documents. Disambiguating which referent is correct and expanding the surface form are separate operations — perform only the former. Source-span spelling and near-verbatim extraction (ae-00001) outrank full-name canonicalization (misc-00003), which applies only when the ground truth/source itself stores the fuller name. This extends misc-00035 beyond pipe-delimited bare-surname fields to natural-language contexts where disambiguation reflex, not surname-expansion, drives the over-canonicalization error.
[misc-00048] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For passive eponym frames of the form 'This [thing] was named for/after [person anchor]' (e.g., 'This programming language was named for calculating-machine inventor Blaise'), the demonstrative head names the slot: the thing that carries the name, not the namesake person. Treat the 'named for' phrase's person ('calculating-machine inventor Blaise') as a search anchor identifying the namesake, locate the sentence mapping the thing to that anchor (e.g., 'the Pascal programming language was named ... for Blaise Pascal'), and return the minimal bare span that fills the head (e.g., 'Pascal') exactly as spelled in the source — never the person's fuller name ('Blaise Pascal') and never the person's role/descriptor. Case is normalized (misc-00011), so don't chase ground-truth capitalization. This inverts misc-00036 (there the slot was the namesake person and the named thing was the anchor) and complements misc-00023 (active-voice 'X named this Y for [related-entity]' where the anchor is a non-namesake distractor).
[misc-00049] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: When a source/answer field is truncated mid-name (e.g., a StudyStack flashcard answer field cut off at 'SOUTH SEA...' for a 'this "bubble"' clue), do NOT emit the visible fragment under shortest-span extraction (ae-00001) and do NOT treat the missing head noun as a subtractable trailing modifier (misc-00004). Complete the full multi-word proper name from cross-document repetition of the canonical entity ('South Sea Bubble' / 'the South Sea Bubble') and return it bare and unformatted. The leading article is droppable under exact-match normalization; the content-bearing head noun ('Bubble') is integral stored answer content and must never be cut. This extends misc-00035 (pipe-delimited flashcard fields outrank heuristics) to truncated fields, and reinforces misc-00028's rule that a common-noun head inside a proper name is integral, not droppable.
[misc-00050] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For plural-slot clues of the form 'Y comes from these animals' / 'these X' where the context lists several candidate X (e.g., sheep, goat, cattle, hogs, horses, mules, donkeys), plural phrasing does not license returning the full list or a compound like 'sheep or goat intestines'. Locate the emphasis marker that singles out one primary member ('particularly sheep', 'usually use sheep or goat intestines', 'especially X') and return that minimal bare singular span exactly as spelled in the source ('sheep'), never the list or the compound. The stored ground truth is the single primary exemplar; over-extraction is the real failure mode. This extends misc-00022 from synonym-set disambiguation to multi-member list disambiguation, and complements misc-00045 (bare list member selection) by anchoring the choice to the emphasis marker rather than list position.
texts.ad3046719b53b31428cce1705c31a87863ea5d0a:
Before answering each question, invoke the Skill tool with skill "flashrsi:searchqa" and follow that skill. Then answer the question in the requested format.


<!-- flashrsi:ace-playbook -->
## OTHERS
[ae-00001] helpful=97 harmful=6 :: When the context states the answer near-verbatim, return the shortest entity span that fully satisfies the clue (e.g., 'Amazon' for 'the Amazon'). Article omission is safe because exact-match evaluation normalizes the two as equivalent.
[misc-00002] helpful=13 harmful=1 :: When a clue uses a nickname or descriptive phrase (e.g., 'The Happiest Place on Earth'), search the context for an explicit appositive or parenthetical that names the canonical entity, and return that minimal named entity rather than the descriptive phrase.
[misc-00003] helpful=7 harmful=10 :: For nickname- or slogan-based clues (e.g., 'Ike' / 'I Like Ike'), return the complete canonical multi-word name exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth (e.g., 'Dwight D. Eisenhower'). Do not shorten to a surname like 'Eisenhower' or return the descriptive phrase 'I Like Ike', as either can break exact-match scoring.
[misc-00004] helpful=2 harmful=2 :: For slot-filling clues that embed part of the canonical name in the question — especially as a quoted trailing modifier (e.g., Bret Harte wrote about these exiles "of Poker Flat") — treat the quoted material as known context, not answer content. Subtract it and return only the complementary minimal head span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'The Outcasts', not 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'). Do not over-apply the 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' heuristic to these clues; that rule is for nickname/slogan clues where no part of the name is already supplied.
[misc-00005] helpful=87 harmful=0 :: When the prompt says 'Return only the short answer,' emit the bare plain-text entity with no markdown, emphasis, or punctuation decoration (e.g., 'Bob Mackie', never '**Bob Mackie**'). Output-format correctness is an independent axis from content correctness: a lenient scorer may normalize markdown, but strict exact-match or pipeline scoring may not, so always return the minimal unformatted span.
[misc-00006] helpful=49 harmful=2 :: When the clue is a demonstrative coreference such as 'this institution' / 'this X' (no explicit named entity in the question), resolve the referent from the context — the canonical named entity repeatedly linked to the subject across documents — and return that minimal span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'Smithsonian Institution'), bare and unformatted. This extends the shortest-span and bare-output rules to coreference resolution rather than near-verbatim extraction.
[misc-00007] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the question contains a typo (e.g., 'Led Zeppellin' for 'Led Zeppelin'), do not propagate the question's misspelling into the answer. Copy the named entity exactly as spelled in the source/ground truth — source spelling is authoritative. This extends ae-00001: near-verbatim extraction uses the source span, not the question's (possibly misspelled) wording.
[misc-00008] helpful=3 harmful=0 :: In this dataset, context documents sometimes embed the clue and its answer as a single pipe-delimited pair (e.g., '...this late Led Zeppellin drummer | John Bonham'). When resolving a demonstrative coreference ('this X'), check for the referent immediately after the '|' separator and return that minimal entity span bare and unformatted — a concrete delimiter signal that extends misc-00006.
[misc-00009] helpful=1 harmful=1 :: When a fill-in-the-blank sits inside a multi-word proper noun and the source states the full name verbatim, return the complete canonical entity exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Funk & Wagnalls', not just the blank-filler 'Funk'). Reserve fragment subtraction (misc-00004) for quoted descriptive modifiers genuinely external to the named entity; an inseparable component like '& Wagnalls' is part of the entity, and when the ground truth stores the full name, full-entity near-verbatim extraction beats literal blank-filling.
[misc-00010] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For reversal/reference clues of the form 'X refers to Y as this' (the question already names one entity and asks what it is referred to as), the answer is stated verbatim in the inverse sentence in the context (e.g., 'What Americans refer to as Swiss cheese, a Swiss person would call Emmentaler'). Return the minimal bare span that fills 'this' (e.g., 'Swiss cheese'), and do not echo the clue's own named entity (e.g., Emmentaler) or a longer descriptive phrase.
[misc-00011] helpful=8 harmful=0 :: Exact-match scoring normalizes case, so capitalization is not a risk axis: a correct source span is safe in any case ('man-hour' == 'Man-hour'). Do not alter a correct answer or spend effort matching ground-truth case; the real risks remain over-extraction and formatting decoration.
[misc-00012] helpful=8 harmful=1 :: For definitional clues of the form 'X means Y' (the question supplies the gloss/meaning and asks for the name), return the named entity X that the context explicitly glosses — not the gloss Y (e.g., 'Soyuz', not 'union'). Locate the sentence mapping the gloss to the name, extract the minimal canonical span verbatim from the source, and emit it bare and unformatted. Case and article differences are normalized by exact-match scoring; over-extraction and markdown decoration remain the real risks.
[misc-00013] helpful=4 harmful=0 :: For 'In this book/this work...' slot-filling clues, read the phrase as requesting the work's title. Locate the sentence in the context that names the book and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled in the source (e.g., 'Great Expectations'), omitting the author, year, or any longer descriptive wrapper. Emit it as plain text with no markdown or punctuation.
[misc-00014] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: Minimal-span near-verbatim extraction is robust even when the question's factual premise is loose or inaccurate (e.g., saying Miss Havisham 'dies' when the source states she survives as an invalid). Identify the slot actually being probed (here, the book title) and return the shortest exact source span; do not over-extract, correct the premise, or get derailed by premise accuracy.
[misc-00015] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the clue quotes an exact source line and asks about 'this X' (e.g., '"This door you might not open, and you did" begins a Millay poem about this folklore guy'), treat the quoted line as a search anchor: locate that verbatim line in the context and return the minimal named-entity tag or appositive adjacent to it (e.g., 'Bluebeard'), not the quoted line itself or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00006 — coreference resolution is anchored by the quoted line rather than by repetition across documents.
[misc-00016] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For 'this way'-style demonstrative slot-filling clues where the referent is a plain adverb or verb-phrase complement rather than a named entity, apply the same minimal near-verbatim extraction: locate the verbatim filler in the source (e.g., 'backwards' in 'play a country song backwards') and return that shortest bare span, not the full verb phrase. This extends misc-00006 beyond named-entity referents to adverbial fillers; case differences remain safe (misc-00011).
[misc-00017] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the canonical entity or title contains distinctive internal punctuation (e.g., 'M*A*S*H'), return the full stylized form exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth, preserving the punctuation. Do not treat meaningful punctuation as decoration to strip under the minimal-span/plain-text rules; those rules target markdown/formatting and case/article normalization, not the entity's own written form. Prefer the stylized rendering over a shorter unpunctuated variant even when both appear in the context.
[misc-00018] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For metalinguistic clues about a word or name's spelling/property (e.g., 'this state's name is missing one of its Ns', 'X is misspelled on...'), the context often embeds the entity in a 'The word X ...' / 'The name X ...' frame. Return X — the minimal span immediately after 'word'/'name' — bare and unformatted, not the predicate or the question's paraphrase. Extends misc-00006: the demonstrative referent resolves to the entity inside the metalinguistic frame rather than via cross-document repetition.
[misc-00019] helpful=10 harmful=1 :: For 'this X' demonstrative clues that already name specific anchor entities in the question (e.g., 'born in Itawamba County in this state, not far from Elvis' birthplace, Tupelo'), treat the named county/town as search anchors, not answer content. Return only the minimal co-located entity that fills the 'this X' slot (e.g., 'Mississippi'), bare and unformatted — never a longer wrapper like 'Itawamba County, Mississippi' or an echo of the anchors. This extends misc-00006, which covered clues with no named entity in the question.
[misc-00020] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: When a clue has the form 'this [author] bestseller [plot detail]' (e.g., '...this Erich Segal bestseller'), treat the named author and any character names as search anchors, not answer content. The slot asks for the work's title: locate it verbatim in the context and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Love Story'), never the author ('Erich Segal'), a character echo, or a longer wrapper like 'Erich Segal's Love Story'. This extends misc-00013 to author-anchored bestseller phrasing.
[misc-00021] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'this [year] film' demonstrative clues that pair a named actor with a defining descriptor or pun (e.g., 'To Dustin Hoffman this '82 film was a "drag"'), treat the actor, the year, and the descriptor as search anchors, not answer content: the slot asks for the film title. Locate the title that is repeatedly co-located with those anchors in the context and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Tootsie'), never the actor ('Dustin Hoffman'), the descriptor ('drag'), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00020 from author-anchored bestsellers to year/actor-anchored film clues and flags the descriptor/pun as a distracter.
[misc-00022] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: For 'It's [definition]' definitional clues (the question supplies a gloss and asks for the term), when the context offers multiple synonymous candidate terms that all fit the gloss (e.g., 'bleat' vs 'baa' for the cry of a sheep/goat), return the term most repeatedly and directly linked to the gloss across documents (e.g., 'bleat'), bare and unformatted — not an alternate synonym. This extends misc-00012, which covered gloss-to-name extraction but not synonym disambiguation; distracter list documents naming several terms do not change the answer, which is the dominant repeated source term.
[misc-00023] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'X named this Y for/after [descriptive anchor]' clues (e.g., 'Marie Curie named this element for her native land'), the descriptive anchor resolves to a related but different entity (Poland) and is a distractor, not the answer. Locate the verbatim 'named X in honour/after [anchor]' frame in the source and return the minimal named entity X (e.g., 'polonium'), bare and unformatted — never the anchor entity (the native land) or any alternative/distractor element name.
[misc-00024] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For definitional clues of the form 'Term for the X that...' where the gloss defines a single head noun but the context also repeatedly uses a fuller compound (modifier + head, e.g., 'speech balloon'), return only the minimal head noun the definition directly glosses (e.g., 'balloon'), bare and unformatted. The modifier belongs to the complete device/object, not the thing the definition targets, so a frequent co-located compound must not override minimal-span extraction. This extends misc-00012/misc-00022 and guards against mis-applying misc-00003's 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' heuristic to non-nickname definitional slots.
[misc-00025] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'They were once called [quoted nickname]' / historical-renaming clues (e.g., 'They were once called "Saratoga Chips" after the town...'), treat the quoted nickname as a search anchor pointing to the referent, not as the answer. Resolve the pronoun to the current canonical name of the thing — often a common noun repeatedly stated in the context ('potato chips') — and return that minimal bare span exactly as spelled in the source, never the historical nickname or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00002 to past-tense renaming frames where the target is a common noun rather than a proper named entity, and extends misc-00006 to pronoun-resolved referents.
[misc-00026] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'this author's tales: "X" & "Y"' / Jeopardy-style clues that name the works and ask for the author (the inverse of misc-00020/misc-00021), treat the quoted titles as search anchors, not answer content. Locate the verbatim clue in the context — often reproduced in a flashcard/pair line with the answer appended after a comma — and return the minimal author name co-located with it (e.g., 'Wally Lamb'), bare and unformatted; never echo a book title or a longer wrapper. Near-verbatim adjacency outranks any temptation to answer with a title.
[misc-00027] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: When the source and ground truth consistently render a person's name with an honorific or title (e.g., 'Sir Isaac Newton'), return the complete canonical form exactly as it appears in the source, preserving the honorific. Apply minimal-span stripping only to droppable function words that exact-match scoring normalizes (e.g., 'the', 'a'), never to honorifics or titles that are integral name content — 'Sir Isaac Newton' and 'Isaac Newton' are different answers under exact match. This bounds ae-00001/misc-00006: the 'shortest span' rule does not authorize dropping title content embedded in the stored name.
[misc-00028] helpful=1 harmful=0 :: For 'gave it this name' / naming-frame slots that target a publication or journal title (e.g., 'Forbes magazine'), the full multi-word name is the answer. A common-noun component like 'magazine' is integral name content stored in the source and ground truth, not a droppable function word that exact-match scoring normalizes away (unlike 'the'/'a'). Return the complete compound exactly as spelled in the source, bare and unformatted; do not strip 'magazine' or any other title component. This extends misc-00009's 'full entity beats blank-filler' rule to publication-title slots and bounds ae-00001's shortest-span rule against dropping non-article title content.
[misc-00029] helpful=0 harmful=1 :: For 'X is a [modifier] type of this [category]' hypernym clues (e.g., 'neoprene is a synthetic type of this material'), the question supplies the specific term X and asks for its category noun. Locate the verbatim definitional sentence and return the minimal category head noun exactly as stated in the source ('rubber'), bare and unformatted — never the defined term X ('neoprene'/'polychloroprene') and never the fuller modifier+compound ('synthetic rubber'). This inverts misc-00012 (there the gloss was supplied and the name was the slot; here the name is supplied and the hypernym is the slot) and extends misc-00024's head-noun-over-compound rule to the 'type of this Y' frame.
[misc-00030] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For multi-step process clues like 'Before X, Y is cleaned with this [misleading descriptor] acid' (e.g., galvanizing's 'very caustic acid'), treat the descriptor as a step indicator, not literal answer content: 'caustic' belongs to the alkali cleaning stage, while the noun 'acid' selects the acid-pickling stage. When two candidate acids appear in the context, return the one stated most directly and repeatedly as the pickling acid (e.g., 'hydrochloric acid'), exactly as spelled, bare and unformatted — never the cross-step alkali substance ('caustic soda'), the generic head noun ('acid'), or a one-off paired alternative ('sulfuric acid'). Extends misc-00022 from synonymous candidates to competing non-synonym candidates and cross-step distractors.
[misc-00031] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative title-slot clues of the form 'This [descriptor] series with [actor] was based on [author]'s [autobiography]' (a media-adaptation frame), treat the actor and the source author/autobiography as search anchors, not answer content. Locate the sentence in the context that names the series and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled in the source (e.g., 'Eight Is Enough'), never the actor, the author, the source-work type, or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00020/misc-00021 from author-bestseller and actor-film frames to actor-plus-source-material TV-series frames; case differences remain normalized (misc-00011), so the real risks stay over-extraction and formatting decoration.
[misc-00032] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative 'this person' clues that name a comparable exemplar via 'like X' (e.g., 'like Ben Bradlee'), the slot resolves to the role/title noun the exemplar holds in the context (e.g., 'editor'), not the exemplar's proper name ('Ben Bradlee') or a fuller role phrase ('editor of The Washington Post'). Return the minimal bare head noun with the article dropped — article omission is safe under exact-match normalization ('editor' == 'The editor'). This extends misc-00006/misc-00019: the referent is a common-noun role rather than a named entity, and the anchor arrives as a 'like' comparison pointing to the exemplar's role, not as the answer itself.
[misc-00033] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For definitional clues where the question paraphrases the dictionary gloss with a gerund or participle (e.g., 'following a winding & turning course'), match the answer's morphological form to the clue's own grammatical phrasing. A gerund/participle phrasing selects the -ing form (e.g., 'Meandering', as in the source title 'Meandering river'), not the base verb ('meander') that the dictionary's infinitive gloss ('to follow') superficially points to. Derivational suffixes are word-forming, not droppable function words: the 'shortest span' rule (ae-00001) trims articles/wrappers, never suffixes, and 'meander' vs 'meandering' are distinct strings under exact match. Return the exact -ing span verbatim from the source, bare and unformatted.
[misc-00034] helpful=0 harmful=1 :: For 'this character answers to [appellation]' clues (e.g., 'answers to "Gloucester"'), the appellation/title is a search anchor and disambiguator, not the answer. When the same title is shared by multiple referents across documents (e.g., Gloucester in King Lear, Richard II, and Richard III), use the premise clause (e.g., 'begins as duke of Gloucester, not king') to select the correct referent, then return the character's canonical name stated verbatim in the source (e.g., 'Richard III'), bare and unformatted — never the appellation ('Gloucester') or a fuller title phrase ('Duke of Gloucester'). Extends misc-00025/misc-00002 (title-as-anchor) to same-titled referents requiring premise-based disambiguation.
[misc-00035] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: In pipe-delimited Jeopardy flashcard contexts (structure [category] | [clue] | [answer]), the token after the final '|' is the stored answer and outranks all canonicalization heuristics. When that answer field is a bare surname (e.g., 'Clark'), return it verbatim — do NOT expand it to the full name ('Wesley Clark') even if the 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' instinct (misc-00003) fires. misc-00003 applies only when the ground truth/source itself stores the full multi-word name; a surname-only ground truth is a distinct pattern where full-name expansion turns correct entity identification into an exact-match failure. Explicit minimal answer spans and delimiter signals always outrank canonicalization heuristics.
[misc-00036] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For eponym/namesake demonstrative clues of the form '[Named place/thing] includes a [thing] named for this [descriptor] [role/figure]' (e.g., 'a museum named for this Civil War figure'), the slot asks for the namesake person or entity, not the named thing. Treat the named place/thing in the question as the search anchor, locate the sentence co-locating that anchor with a proper name (e.g., '...learn about John Brown, a figure who is...'), and return the minimal canonical name verbatim from the source, bare and unformatted — never the descriptive role ('Civil War figure'), the named thing ('museum'), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00019 from locative anchors ('born in X in this state') to the 'named for this person' eponym frame, and complements misc-00023, which covers the inverse direction (the thing named after an anchor).
[misc-00037] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For pipe-delimited Jeopardy flashcards whose final '|' field is a bare common-noun title or role shared by several named persons (e.g., 'Title held ... by Balbinus, Bao Dai & Bidatsu | Emperor'), the stored answer field is the complete answer. Return it verbatim and unformatted ('Emperor'); do NOT concatenate it with a named anchor from the clue ('Emperor Bidatsu') or expand to a longer phrase. The named persons are search anchors, not answer content. This extends misc-00035 beyond bare-surname fields to bare title/common-noun fields, where the failure mode is name-title concatenation rather than full-name expansion.
[misc-00038] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When a clue appends a trailing abbreviation or code (IATA airport, postal, or state code) after a slogan or phrase — e.g., 'Let freedom ring: PHL' — decode the code as a decisive location signal, not noise. The format '[slogan]: [location code]' asks for the location the code points to, not the salient iconic object co-located with the slogan (return 'Philadelphia', never 'Liberty Bell'). This extends misc-00019 (named anchors as search anchors) to abbreviated codes, which disambiguate between co-located candidate spans that shortest-span extraction alone cannot choose between.
[misc-00039] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For leading-ellipsis fill-in-the-blank clues of the form '"...fragment"' (e.g., '"...on my mind"'), the leading ellipsis marks a missing leading token, so the supplied fragment is known context to subtract, not the topic. Scan the context for verbatim phrases of the form 'X fragment', subtract the supplied tail, and return only the minimal complementary head exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'Georgia' from 'Georgia on my mind') — never the full title ('Georgia on My Mind'), the salient co-occurring entity (Ellie Goulding), or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00004 to leading-ellipsis slots and warns that cross-document entity salience/frequency is a distractor when the clue is a completion rather than a topic query; fragment subtraction overrides full-name canonicalization (misc-00003/misc-00009) whenever the ground truth stores only the head.
[misc-00040] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When a holiday/date name appears both with a leading 'St.' prefix (e.g., 'St. Valentine's Day' in an anchor sentence) and without it (the dominant bare form 'Valentine's Day' repeated across titles/bodies), and the ground truth stores the bare form, return the minimal bare form — do NOT over-apply misc-00027's honorific-preservation rule. misc-00027 protects personal honorifics ('Sir Isaac Newton') that are integral to the stored name; the 'St.' saint-prefix is a variant form, and shortest-span extraction (ae-00001) selects 'Valentine's Day', not 'St. Valentine's Day'.
[misc-00041] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For possessive-frame clues of the form '[Nickname] was the [object] of this [descriptor/person]' (e.g., 'Tick-Licker was the favorite rifle of this 18th century Kentucky frontiersman'), the nickname and the object are search anchors, not answer content — the slot is the possessor. Locate the attributive sentence in the source (e.g., 'Daniel Boone had a rifle that was known as the "Tick-licker"') and return the owner's full canonical name verbatim, bare and unformatted; never the nickname, the object ('rifle'), or a surname-only shortening. This extends misc-00002/misc-00006: the nickname names a possession rather than the target itself, so resolve nickname → object → possessor; descriptor typos remain distractors (misc-00007).
[misc-00042] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For wordplay-reversal clues (spoonerisms, malapropisms, eggcorns), the question embeds a mangled phrase and asks for the corrected phrase; the co-located named entity the phrase refers to is a distractor. Detect the reversal by transposed initial consonant clusters (e.g., 'queer old dean' → 'dear old queen') and locate the explicit correction pairing in the source — a bracket ('[dear old queen]') or contrastive frame ('instead of to "our dear old Queen"'). Return the corrected phrase verbatim and bare, never the referent ('Queen Victoria') and never the mangled form. Corrected-phrase extraction from the contrastive signal outranks entity-extraction heuristics (misc-00002) and canonicalization; misc-00025 (mangled form as anchor, return corrected current form) points the right way but is scoped to historical renaming, not phonetic transposition.
[misc-00043] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For bare possessive-pronoun slots in natural-language media clues of the form '"[Track]" is the last song on his [year] album "[Album]"' (the question never states a role like 'this artist'), treat the track and album titles as search anchors, resolve the possessive pronoun to the artist/creator explicitly named in the context (e.g., 'Let's Dance is the fifteenth studio album by David Bowie'), and return the minimal canonical name span bare and unformatted — never the album, the track, or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00026 from 'this author's tales' (explicit-role, Jeopardy-style named-works to author) to bare possessive-pronoun media clues where the creator role is implicit and must be inferred from the possessive object.
[misc-00044] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For acronym-based demonstrative clues ('If your TV has PIP, it has this feature'), the acronym is a search anchor, not answer content: the slot asks for its full expansion. Locate the explicit expansion in the context — typically a near-verbatim appositive/parenthetical like 'Picture in Picture (PIP)' — and return the complete canonical expansion exactly as spelled in the source, bare and unformatted (e.g., 'Picture in Picture'). Never return the acronym itself ('PIP') or a partial form. This extends misc-00002 (nickname → parenthetical canonical entity) and misc-00038 (code-as-anchor) to term/feature acronyms where the answer is the expanded phrase, not a location or nickname.
[misc-00045] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For a bare, interrogative-free comma-separated list of named entities (e.g., 'Minsk, Monrovia, Manama'), treat it as a member-selection slot, not a classification slot: return the single listed member the ground truth stores (here 'Minsk'), bare and unformatted. Never emit the shared category/hypernym (e.g., 'capital cities'), even when a context document title offers it near-verbatim — salient category labels are distractors here. Bounds ae-00001 (shortest-span extraction toward a verbatim category title) and misc-00029 (hypernym reflex), which both misfire on bare co-hyponym lists.
[misc-00046] helpful=2 harmful=0 :: For demonstrative clues whose head is the medium itself ('this musical', 'this film', 'this book') and which also embed an actor, a descriptor/pun, a venue, and a year, the medium head requests the work's title: locate the opening definitional sentence of the form 'X is a [medium]' in the context (e.g., 'The King and I is a musical') — this is the highest-confidence evidence and directly yields the minimal bare title span. Treat every co-located anchor (the actor, the 'regal' pun, the theatre, the year) as distractors that confirm rather than replace the title; never return an anchor, the pun, or a longer wrapper. Preserve any article that is part of the stored title (e.g., 'The King and I'), per misc-00028. This extends misc-00021 from 'this [year] film' actor+descriptor frames to medium-as-head frames and adds the definitional-sentence signal plus venue anchor.
[misc-00047] helpful=3 harmful=0 :: When the clue and/or the source sentence already names the answer with a bare name (e.g., 'George Bush' in both the announcement sentence and the clue 'that George Bush won the election'), return that exact minimal span verbatim. Do NOT expand it to a fuller disambiguated variant ('George H. W. Bush') merely because the corpus contains homonymous entities ('George W. Bush') or fuller forms of the same person in other documents. Disambiguating which referent is correct and expanding the surface form are separate operations — perform only the former. Source-span spelling and near-verbatim extraction (ae-00001) outrank full-name canonicalization (misc-00003), which applies only when the ground truth/source itself stores the fuller name. This extends misc-00035 beyond pipe-delimited bare-surname fields to natural-language contexts where disambiguation reflex, not surname-expansion, drives the over-canonicalization error.
[misc-00048] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For passive eponym frames of the form 'This [thing] was named for/after [person anchor]' (e.g., 'This programming language was named for calculating-machine inventor Blaise'), the demonstrative head names the slot: the thing that carries the name, not the namesake person. Treat the 'named for' phrase's person ('calculating-machine inventor Blaise') as a search anchor identifying the namesake, locate the sentence mapping the thing to that anchor (e.g., 'the Pascal programming language was named ... for Blaise Pascal'), and return the minimal bare span that fills the head (e.g., 'Pascal') exactly as spelled in the source — never the person's fuller name ('Blaise Pascal') and never the person's role/descriptor. Case is normalized (misc-00011), so don't chase ground-truth capitalization. This inverts misc-00036 (there the slot was the namesake person and the named thing was the anchor) and complements misc-00023 (active-voice 'X named this Y for [related-entity]' where the anchor is a non-namesake distractor).
[misc-00049] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When a source/answer field is truncated mid-name (e.g., a StudyStack flashcard answer field cut off at 'SOUTH SEA...' for a 'this "bubble"' clue), do NOT emit the visible fragment under shortest-span extraction (ae-00001) and do NOT treat the missing head noun as a subtractable trailing modifier (misc-00004). Complete the full multi-word proper name from cross-document repetition of the canonical entity ('South Sea Bubble' / 'the South Sea Bubble') and return it bare and unformatted. The leading article is droppable under exact-match normalization; the content-bearing head noun ('Bubble') is integral stored answer content and must never be cut. This extends misc-00035 (pipe-delimited flashcard fields outrank heuristics) to truncated fields, and reinforces misc-00028's rule that a common-noun head inside a proper name is integral, not droppable.
[misc-00050] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For plural-slot clues of the form 'Y comes from these animals' / 'these X' where the context lists several candidate X (e.g., sheep, goat, cattle, hogs, horses, mules, donkeys), plural phrasing does not license returning the full list or a compound like 'sheep or goat intestines'. Locate the emphasis marker that singles out one primary member ('particularly sheep', 'usually use sheep or goat intestines', 'especially X') and return that minimal bare singular span exactly as spelled in the source ('sheep'), never the list or the compound. The stored ground truth is the single primary exemplar; over-extraction is the real failure mode. This extends misc-00022 from synonym-set disambiguation to multi-member list disambiguation, and complements misc-00045 (bare list member selection) by anchoring the choice to the emphasis marker rather than list position.
texts.ad440994699746f6cb18ec0c7478e01be8f7ffad:
Before answering each question, invoke the Skill tool with skill "flashrsi:searchqa" and follow that skill. Then answer the question in the requested format.


<!-- flashrsi:ace-playbook -->
## OTHERS
[ae-00001] helpful=163 harmful=12 :: When the context states the answer near-verbatim, return the shortest entity span that fully satisfies the clue (e.g., 'Amazon' for 'the Amazon'). Article omission is safe because exact-match evaluation normalizes the two as equivalent.
[misc-00002] helpful=21 harmful=2 :: When a clue uses a nickname or descriptive phrase (e.g., 'The Happiest Place on Earth'), search the context for an explicit appositive or parenthetical that names the canonical entity, and return that minimal named entity rather than the descriptive phrase.
[misc-00003] helpful=13 harmful=12 :: For nickname- or slogan-based clues (e.g., 'Ike' / 'I Like Ike'), return the complete canonical multi-word name exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth (e.g., 'Dwight D. Eisenhower'). Do not shorten to a surname like 'Eisenhower' or return the descriptive phrase 'I Like Ike', as either can break exact-match scoring.
[misc-00004] helpful=4 harmful=2 :: For slot-filling clues that embed part of the canonical name in the question — especially as a quoted trailing modifier (e.g., Bret Harte wrote about these exiles "of Poker Flat") — treat the quoted material as known context, not answer content. Subtract it and return only the complementary minimal head span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'The Outcasts', not 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'). Do not over-apply the 'return the complete canonical multi-word name' heuristic to these clues; that rule is for nickname/slogan clues where no part of the name is already supplied.
[misc-00005] helpful=151 harmful=0 :: When the prompt says 'Return only the short answer,' emit the bare plain-text entity with no markdown, emphasis, or punctuation decoration (e.g., 'Bob Mackie', never '**Bob Mackie**'). Output-format correctness is an independent axis from content correctness: a lenient scorer may normalize markdown, but strict exact-match or pipeline scoring may not, so always return the minimal unformatted span.
[misc-00006] helpful=85 harmful=4 :: When the clue is a demonstrative coreference such as 'this institution' / 'this X' (no explicit named entity in the question), resolve the referent from the context — the canonical named entity repeatedly linked to the subject across documents — and return that minimal span exactly as it appears in the source (e.g., 'Smithsonian Institution'), bare and unformatted. This extends the shortest-span and bare-output rules to coreference resolution rather than near-verbatim extraction.
[misc-00007] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the question contains a typo (e.g., 'Led Zeppellin' for 'Led Zeppelin'), do not propagate the question's misspelling into the answer. Copy the named entity exactly as spelled in the source/ground truth — source spelling is authoritative. This extends ae-00001: near-verbatim extraction uses the source span, not the question's (possibly misspelled) wording.
[misc-00008] helpful=6 harmful=0 :: In this dataset, context documents sometimes embed the clue and its answer as a single pipe-delimited pair (e.g., '...this late Led Zeppellin drummer | John Bonham'). When resolving a demonstrative coreference ('this X'), check for the referent immediately after the '|' separator and return that minimal entity span bare and unformatted — a concrete delimiter signal that extends misc-00006.
[misc-00009] helpful=1 harmful=1 :: When a fill-in-the-blank sits inside a multi-word proper noun and the source states the full name verbatim, return the complete canonical entity exactly as spelled (e.g., 'Funk & Wagnalls', not just the blank-filler 'Funk'). Reserve fragment subtraction (misc-00004) for quoted descriptive modifiers genuinely external to the named entity; an inseparable component like '& Wagnalls' is part of the entity, and when the ground truth stores the full name, full-entity near-verbatim extraction beats literal blank-filling.
[misc-00010] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For reversal/reference clues of the form 'X refers to Y as this' (the question already names one entity and asks what it is referred to as), the answer is stated verbatim in the inverse sentence in the context (e.g., 'What Americans refer to as Swiss cheese, a Swiss person would call Emmentaler'). Return the minimal bare span that fills 'this' (e.g., 'Swiss cheese'), and do not echo the clue's own named entity (e.g., Emmentaler) or a longer descriptive phrase.
[misc-00011] helpful=20 harmful=0 :: Exact-match scoring normalizes case, so capitalization is not a risk axis: a correct source span is safe in any case ('man-hour' == 'Man-hour'). Do not alter a correct answer or spend effort matching ground-truth case; the real risks remain over-extraction and formatting decoration.
[misc-00012] helpful=17 harmful=2 :: For definitional clues of the form 'X means Y' (the question supplies the gloss/meaning and asks for the name), return the named entity X that the context explicitly glosses — not the gloss Y (e.g., 'Soyuz', not 'union'). Locate the sentence mapping the gloss to the name, extract the minimal canonical span verbatim from the source, and emit it bare and unformatted. Case and article differences are normalized by exact-match scoring; over-extraction and markdown decoration remain the real risks.
[misc-00013] helpful=6 harmful=0 :: For 'In this book/this work...' slot-filling clues, read the phrase as requesting the work's title. Locate the sentence in the context that names the book and return the minimal bare title span exactly as spelled in the source (e.g., 'Great Expectations'), omitting the author, year, or any longer descriptive wrapper. Emit it as plain text with no markdown or punctuation.
[misc-00014] helpful=4 harmful=0 :: Minimal-span near-verbatim extraction is robust even when the question's factual premise is loose or inaccurate (e.g., saying Miss Havisham 'dies' when the source states she survives as an invalid). Identify the slot actually being probed (here, the book title) and return the shortest exact source span; do not over-extract, correct the premise, or get derailed by premise accuracy.
[misc-00015] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the clue quotes an exact source line and asks about 'this X' (e.g., '"This door you might not open, and you did" begins a Millay poem about this folklore guy'), treat the quoted line as a search anchor: locate that verbatim line in the context and return the minimal named-entity tag or appositive adjacent to it (e.g., 'Bluebeard'), not the quoted line itself or a longer wrapper. This extends misc-00006 — coreference resolution is anchored by the quoted line rather than by repetition across documents.
[misc-00016] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For 'this way'-style demonstrative slot-filling clues where the referent is a plain adverb or verb-phrase complement rather than a named entity, apply the same minimal near-verbatim extraction: locate the verbatim filler in the source (e.g., 'backwards' in 'play a country song backwards') and return that shortest bare span, not the full verb phrase. This extends misc-00006 beyond named-entity referents to adverbial fillers; case differences remain safe (misc-00011).
[misc-00017] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: When the canonical entity or title contains distinctive internal punctuation (e.g., 'M*A*S*H'), return the full stylized form exactly as it appears in the source and ground truth, preserving the punctuation. Do not treat meaningful punctuation as decoration to strip under the minimal-span/plain-text rules; those rules target markdown/formatting and case/article normalization, not the entity's own written form. Prefer the stylized rendering over a shorter unpunctuated variant even when both appear in the context.
[misc-00018] helpful=0 harmful=0 :: For metalinguistic clues about a word or name's spelling/property (e.g., 'this state's name is missing one of its Ns', 'X is misspelled on...'), the context often embeds the entity in a 'The word X ...' / 'The name X ...' frame. Return X — the minimal span immediately after 'word'/'name' — bare and unformatted, not the predicate or the question's paraphrase. Extends misc-00006: the demonstrative referent resolves to the entity inside the metalinguistic frame rather than via cross-document repetition.
[misc-00019] helpful=22 harmful=1 :: For 'this X' demonstrative clues that already name specific anchor entities in the question (e.g., 'born in Itawamba County in this state, not far from Elvis' birthplace, Tupelo'), treat the named county/town as search anchors, not answer content. Return only the minimal co-located entity that fills the 'this X' slot (e.g., 'Mississippi'), bare and unformatted — never a longer wrapper like 'Itawamba County, Mississippi' or an echo of the anchors. This extends misc-00006, which covered clues with no named entity in the question.
